maths_errors.text: If you prefer, keep x positive throughout by rearranging first.
maths_errors.correction: It is the coefficient of x that must stay positive, not x itself. In this example the answer is x < −4, so x is negative. Reword as: "keep the number in front of x positive by rearranging first".

missing_spec_content.spec_text: solve linear inequalities in one or two variable(s)
missing_spec_content.why: Only one-variable inequalities are taught. There is nothing on inequalities in two variables, such as y > 2x + 1.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: and quadratic inequalities in one variable
missing_spec_content.why: Quadratic inequalities (e.g. x² < 9, or x² − x − 6 > 0 solved by factorising and checking which regions work) are not mentioned anywhere.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: represent the solution set ... using set notation
missing_spec_content.why: Set notation, such as {x : x ≥ 3}, is never introduced.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: represent the solution set ... on a graph
missing_spec_content.why: Showing inequalities as regions on a graph is not taught.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: In graphical work the convention of a dashed line for strict inequalities and a solid line for an included inequality will be required.
missing_spec_content.why: The dashed/solid line convention for graphs is not mentioned.

cases_not_modelled.why: The only worked example divides by a positive number. The sign flip appears only in a common mistake and a key-fact tip, never as a full worked example.
No worked example expands brackets, e.g. 3(x − 2) < 12.
No worked example has a fraction, e.g. (x + 1)/4 ≥ 2.
No worked example solves something like −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 by doing the same operation to all three parts.
Key fact 3 asks the student to list the integers that satisfy −3 < x ≤ 2, but never lists them (−2, −1, 0, 1, 2) or shows the method.

cases_not_modelled.case: strict inequality on a number line (open circle)
cases_not_modelled.why: The only number line drawn is for x ≥ 3, with a closed circle. No example draws an open circle.

cases_not_modelled.case: double inequality on a number line
cases_not_modelled.why: The lesson never shows a number line with two circles joined by a line segment, e.g. for −2 < x ≤ 5.

cases_not_modelled.case: two-variable inequality shown as a region on a graph

density.why: This is a chain of arrows with several steps on one line. The step from 0 < 12 + 3x to 3x > −12 silently subtracts 12 and swaps the two sides (which reverses the symbol), and neither reason is given. A first-time learner will not follow it in one read.

density.text: Dividing (or multiplying) by a negative number reverses the inequality: −2x > 8 → x < −4.
density.why: The arrow hides the actual step, dividing both sides by −2. The working 8 ÷ (−2) = −4 is not shown.

density.text: You solve an inequality using the same inverse operations as an equation — with one critical exception: if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign must flip direction.
density.why: One sentence carries the general method, an exception and a rule. It gives no reason or small example (e.g. 2 < 3 but −2 > −3) to explain why the sign flips.

density.text: For a double inequality such as −3 < x ≤ 2, list the integers satisfying it — remembering to check each endpoint: −3 is excluded (strict <), 2 is included (≤).
density.why: The sentence asks the student to list integers, check endpoints and recall two symbol meanings, but never states the resulting list.

density.text: A double inequality such as −2 < x ≤ 5 means x is between −2 and 5, not including −2 but including 5.
density.why: The same paragraph describes number lines for single inequalities, but never says how this double inequality is drawn (open circle at −2, closed circle at 5, line between them).
